authority.name: National supervisory authorities (coordinated by the EDPB)

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Know How Your Data Is Used
articles.plainSummary: When a company collects your personal information, it must tell you who it is and why it wants the data. It must also say how long it will keep the data and who might receive it. If it got your data from someone else, it must tell you within a month at the latest. This is the foundation of transparency.
articles.personalImpact: Every site and app you touch feeds a hidden profile of you. That profile shapes your prices, your ads, and what a search reveals about you. Data brokers buy and sell it around the clock. Articles 13 and 14 require a company to tell you what it collects and why. That holds even when it got your data from someone else.
articles.professionalLayer: Articles 13 and 14 establish the transparency obligation that underpins the entire GDPR framework. Article 13 applies when personal data is collected directly from the data subject. Article 14 applies when data is obtained indirectly. Article 13 information is due when the data is obtained. Under Article 14, it is due within a reasonable period and at the latest within one month. It is due sooner at the first communication with the person or the first disclosure to another recipient, whichever comes first. Required disclosures include the identity and contact details of the controller, the purposes and legal basis for processing, any legitimate interests relied upon, recipients or categories of recipients, international transfer safeguards, retention periods, and the existence of all data subject rights. Failure to provide this information at collection renders downstream processing legally vulnerable.
articles.responseTimeline: Article 13: when the data is obtained. Article 14: within a reasonable period and at the latest one month. It is earlier at the first communication with you or the first disclosure to another recipient. The earliest applies.

sourceLinks.label: Article 29 Working Party guidelines on transparency (endorsed by the EDPB)

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization have a current, accurate privacy notice that covers all Article 13 and 14 required disclosures, and is it reviewed whenever processing purposes or legal bases change?

gapRemediation.smb: A single privacy notice covering your primary data collection activities is a reasonable starting point. The common gap is a notice drafted once and never updated. Semi-annual review against your actual data flows is recommended.
gapRemediation.midMarket: You likely collect data across multiple channels. Each collection point may need its own layered notice. A central privacy notice inventory helps ensure coverage is complete and consistent.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise transparency programs require a notice management system that maps notices to processing activities in your RoPA. Notices should be versioned, dated, and archived. Changes to processing trigger automated notice review workflows.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to See Your Data
articles.plainSummary: You have the right to ask any company whether they hold personal information about you and, if they do, to receive a copy of it. The company must also tell you why they have it, where they got it, who they have shared it with, and how long they plan to keep it.
articles.personalImpact: That hidden profile stays invisible until you look. Article 15 lets you request a full copy of what a company holds on you. People use it to uncover guesses about their health, income, or politics. It turns an unseen profile into something you can review and challenge.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of whether their personal data is being processed and, where it is, access to that data along with a defined set of supplementary information. This includes purposes of processing, categories of data, the recipients, envisaged retention period, the existence of other data subject rights, the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, and where data was not collected directly from the data subject, the source. The Court of Justice held in 2023 that controllers must name the actual recipients (C-154/21). Categories are enough only where naming them is impossible or the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive. Where Article 22 automated decision-making applies, the person may also learn the logic involved and its likely consequences. The Court requires an explanation of the procedure and principles actually applied (C-203/22, 2025). Trade-secret conflicts go to the supervisory authority or a court to balance. A first copy must be provided free of charge. The most common compliance gap is providing the raw data without the required supplementary information. Regulators treat an incomplete Article 15 response as a failure to fulfill the right.
articles.responseTimeline: One calendar month from receipt. Extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests, with notification to the data subject within the first month.

sourceLinks.label: EDPB Guidelines on the Right of Access

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization's access request process capture all required supplementary information, not just the data itself, but retention periods, recipients, and data sources?

gapRemediation.smb: A structured response template covering all Article 15 supplementary requirements is a reasonable starting point at this scale. The most common gap is providing raw data without the accompanying context. A checklist prevents this. Semi-annual process review is recommended.
gapRemediation.midMarket: At this scale supplementary information requires coordination across teams. A defined internal workflow with named owners for each information category is necessary. Integration with your CRM or customer data system is important as fulfilling requests manually across fragmented systems becomes unsustainable.
gapRemediation.enterprise: A purpose-built DSR platform should handle Article 15 responses systematically, pulling supplementary information from integrated systems. Recipients should map to your RoPA. Data sources should be documented in your data inventory.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Correct Your Data
articles.plainSummary: If a company holds personal information about you that is wrong or incomplete, you have the right to ask them to fix it. The company must act without undue delay. It must also tell anyone it shared the data with, unless that is impossible or takes disproportionate effort.
articles.personalImpact: One wrong entry can quietly upend your life. A mistaken default, a mixed-up record, a debt that was never yours. It can cost you a loan, an apartment, or a job, and no one tells you why. Article 16 lets you require the correction, so decisions rest on accurate information.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 16 requires controllers to correct inaccurate personal data and complete incomplete data upon a data subject's request. The obligation extends beyond factual errors. An incomplete record that creates a misleading picture of an individual is also subject to rectification. Where corrected data has been shared with third parties, the controller must notify those recipients under Article 19 unless doing so is impossible or disproportionately burdensome. This downstream notification obligation is among the most frequently overlooked aspects of Article 16 compliance.
articles.responseTimeline: One calendar month from receipt. Extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests.

crossReferences.label: Article 19: Notification obligation triggered by rectification

articles.assessTrigger: Does your rectification process include a step to notify third-party recipients of corrections, not just updating the record internally?

gapRemediation.smb: Map your data-sharing relationships so you know who needs to be notified when a correction is made. A simple log tracking which vendors receive personal data gives you the foundation for Article 19 compliance. Semi-annual review recommended.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your rectification process needs to include a step that identifies downstream recipients from your data inventory and triggers notification. This requires your RoPA to be accurate and current.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Rectification at enterprise scale requires integration between your DSR platform, data inventory, and vendor management system. Correction events should automatically trigger notification workflows to all identified recipients.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Delete Your Data
articles.plainSummary: You have the right to ask a company to permanently delete your personal information in certain circumstances. Companies may refuse in some cases, such as a legal duty to keep the data or the defence of legal claims.
articles.personalImpact: An old post, a leaked photo, an address a stalker could use. Years on, they still surface in a search and shape how people judge you. Article 17, the right to be forgotten, lets you request that data be erased. You regain a say over what remains attached to your name.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 17 requires erasure without undue delay when one of six grounds applies: the data is no longer necessary for the purpose collected; consent is withdrawn and no other legal basis applies; the data subject objects under Article 21(1) and no overriding legitimate grounds exist, or objects to direct marketing under Article 21(2); processing was unlawful; a legal obligation requires erasure; or the data relates to a child's information society services consent. Erasure is not absolute. Controllers may refuse where retention is necessary for freedom of expression and information, or for a legal obligation or public task. Public health is another ground. So is archiving, research or statistics, where erasure would seriously impair that work. The last ground is the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims. Documenting refusal grounds is as operationally important as fulfilling requests. Backup and archive erasure presents a specific technical challenge that regulators increasingly expect organizations to address explicitly.
articles.responseTimeline: One calendar month from receipt. Extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests.

crossReferences.label: Article 19: Notification obligation triggered by erasure
Article 21: Right to Object grounds overlap

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization have documented grounds for both fulfilling and refusing erasure requests, and is the decision-making process for refusals logged and defensible to a supervisory authority?

gapRemediation.smb: Build a simple decision tree covering the six grounds and exemptions. The most common gap is treating every request as automatically valid. Document outcomes for every request. Semi-annual retention schedule review helps preempt requests.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Erasure becomes technically complex as personal data spans multiple systems. Your process needs to map to your data inventory so deletion triggers across all relevant systems. Backup and archive erasure needs a defined, documented approach.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise erasure requires orchestration across business units and systems including legacy infrastructure. A DSR platform should automate deletion workflows with confirmation logging at each step. Backup erasure schedules should be documented and defensible.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Limit How Your Data Is Used
articles.plainSummary: In certain situations you can ask a company to temporarily stop using your personal information, even if they do not have to delete it. This gives you a way to pause processing while a dispute or legal matter is resolved.
articles.personalImpact: You catch a company using your data in a way that feels wrong. Normally it keeps going while you argue. Article 18 lets you freeze the processing instead. It then pauses until the question is resolved.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 18 allows data subjects to obtain restriction of processing in four circumstances: the accuracy of the data is contested and verification is pending; processing is unlawful but the data subject opposes erasure; the controller no longer needs the data but the data subject requires it for legal claims; or the data subject has objected under Article 21 and verification of overriding grounds is pending. When processing is restricted, data may only be stored, not actively processed, except with the data subject's consent, for legal claims, for protection of another person's rights, or for important public interest reasons. The controller must notify the data subject before lifting a restriction. Restriction requires technical capability to flag and isolate individual records from active processing workflows.
articles.responseTimeline: One calendar month from receipt. Extendable by two further months. Controller must notify data subject before lifting restriction.

crossReferences.label: Article 19: Notification obligation triggered by restriction
Article 21: Right to Object (restriction pending objection outcome)

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization have a technical mechanism to flag individual records as restricted and exclude them from active processing workflows, and a process to notify the data subject before restriction is lifted?

gapRemediation.smb: For simple systems, restriction may mean manually flagging a record and documenting what processing is suspended. A log of restricted records with dates and grounds is a reasonable starting point. Semi-annual review ensures restrictions do not remain in place indefinitely.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Manual flagging becomes unsustainable across multiple systems. Your DSR process should include a defined technical step for restricting records across all relevant platforms. The notification obligation before lifting restriction is frequently missed.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise-scale restriction requires a technical architecture that can isolate individual records across integrated systems including data warehouses. Restricted status should propagate automatically. Lifting restriction should trigger a notification workflow before processing resumes.

articles.surfaceLabel: The Company's Duty to Tell Others When Your Data Changes
articles.plainSummary: When a company corrects, deletes, or restricts your personal information, they must inform anyone else they previously shared it with, unless that is impossible or would require disproportionate effort.
articles.personalImpact: You fix a wrong record, but the company already shared it widely. The old error lives on in systems you cannot see. Article 19 makes it tell every recipient to update or delete it too. A single request reaches the copies you could not track yourself.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 19 is a supporting obligation triggered by three data subject rights: rectification (Article 16), erasure (Article 17), and restriction of processing (Article 18). When any of these actions are taken, the controller must communicate the action to each recipient to whom the data was disclosed, unless notification is impossible or involves disproportionate effort. Controllers must inform the data subject of those recipients upon request. Article 19 compliance depends entirely on the quality of a controller's data sharing records. Organizations that cannot identify who received personal data cannot fulfill this obligation. This makes Article 19 a practical test of data mapping maturity.
articles.assessTrigger: Can your organization identify every recipient that received a specific individual's personal data, and do you have a process to notify those recipients when that data is corrected, erased, or restricted?

gapRemediation.smb: Maintain a simple log of data sharing relationships. When you fulfill a rectification, erasure, or restriction request, check that log and notify relevant parties. Semi-annual review of sharing relationships ensures the log stays current.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your data inventory or RoPA should be the source of truth for recipient identification. Article 19 notifications should be a defined workflow step attached to your DSR fulfillment process.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Automated recipient identification from your RoPA and integrated notification workflows are expected at this scale. Notification completion should be logged and auditable.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Take Your Data Elsewhere
articles.plainSummary: You have the right to receive a copy of your personal information in a format that allows you to transfer it to another company or service. This right exists so that companies cannot lock you in by holding your data hostage.
articles.personalImpact: Your bank, your apps, and your inbox hold years of your life. Leaving usually means abandoning all of it. Article 20 lets you take your data and move it to another provider. You can switch on your own terms rather than lose your history.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 20 grants data subjects the right to receive personal data they have provided to a controller in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and to transmit that data to another controller without hindrance. This right applies only where processing is based on consent or on a contract, and where processing is carried out by automated means. It does not apply to processing based on legitimate interests or legal obligations. Where technically feasible, the data subject may request direct transmission between controllers. Portability applies only to data the individual themselves provided. Inferred or derived data generated by the controller does not fall within scope.
articles.responseTimeline: One calendar month from receipt. Extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests.

sourceLinks.label: Article 29 Working Party guidelines on data portability (endorsed by the EDPB)

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization have the technical capability to export personal data in a structured, machine-readable format, and have you defined what data falls within the scope of portability versus what is excluded as derived data?

gapRemediation.smb: A CSV or JSON export of the data subject's record from your primary system is typically sufficient. Define what data you hold that was provided by the individual versus what you derived. Only the former is portable.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Build consistent export capability across multiple systems. A standard export format should be defined and documented. The legal basis mapping in your RoPA determines which processing activities are subject to portability.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise portability programs require automated export workflows integrated with your DSR platform, with clearly defined data scope boundaries. Direct controller-to-controller transfer capability is increasingly expected by regulators.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Say No to How Your Data Is Used
articles.plainSummary: You have the right to object to a company using your personal information for certain purposes, including direct marketing and profiling. For direct marketing, your objection must always be honored. For other purposes, the right applies when the company relies on its legitimate interests or a public task. You object based on your own situation. The company must then stop, unless it shows compelling grounds or needs the data for legal claims.
articles.personalImpact: A retailer turns one glance at a product into ads that follow you for weeks. Article 21 lets you object to that use of your data. For direct marketing, the company must stop, with no balancing test. The targeting ends once you exercise that right.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 21 grants two distinct objection rights with different legal thresholds. Where processing is based on legitimate interests or public interest, the data subject may object on grounds relating to their particular situation, and the controller must cease processing unless it can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds that override the data subject's interests, or the processing is necessary for legal claims. Where processing is for direct marketing, including profiling related to direct marketing, the right to object is absolute. The data may no longer be processed for marketing, with no balancing test. Controllers must tell data subjects about this right clearly and separately, at the latest at the first communication. The absolute nature of the marketing objection right is frequently underestimated. Many organizations treat it as one factor to weigh rather than a mandatory stop.
articles.responseTimeline: Direct marketing objections: stop processing for marketing without undue delay, and within one month at the latest. Other objections: one calendar month to respond, extendable by two further months.

sourceLinks.label: EDPB Guidelines 1/2024 on legitimate interest (draft for consultation)

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization suppress direct marketing to individuals who have objected, promptly and permanently, and do you have a documented process for handling non-marketing objections that includes a legitimate grounds assessment?

gapRemediation.smb: At minimum, maintain a suppression list for direct marketing objections and ensure it is checked before every marketing send. The marketing suppression obligation is absolute. There is no exception at any scale.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your marketing platform should have native suppression list functionality integrated with your DSR process. Objections received through any channel should update the suppression list automatically.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise marketing suppression requires real-time integration between your DSR platform, CRM, and all marketing execution systems. Non-marketing objection assessments should be documented, reviewed by the DPO, and logged for audit purposes.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right Not to Be Judged by an Algorithm Alone
articles.plainSummary: You have the right not to be subject to a decision made entirely by an automated system with no human involved when that decision significantly affects you. This includes things like automated loan approvals, job application screening, or insurance pricing based solely on algorithms.
articles.personalImpact: You apply for a loan and an algorithm rejects you in seconds. No human looked, and the cause may be a flawed profile you never saw. Article 22 generally bans decisions like this. Where an exception allows one, you can demand a human review and contest the result.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 22(1) sets a general prohibition on decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal or similarly significant effects. The Court of Justice confirmed this reading in SCHUFA (C-634/21, 2023). Three conditions must all be met: there is a decision, it is based solely on automated processing, and it has legal or similarly significant effects. Exceptions exist where the decision is necessary for a contract, authorized by law, or based on explicit consent. For the contract and consent exceptions, the controller must at least offer the data subject human intervention, a chance to express a view, and a way to contest the decision. For decisions authorized by law, that law must set the safeguards. The practical challenge is defining meaningful human involvement. Rubber-stamping automated outputs without genuine review does not count.
articles.responseTimeline: Standard one-month response timeline under Article 12 applies when a data subject contests a decision.

sourceLinks.label: Article 29 Working Party guidelines on automated decision-making and profiling (endorsed by the EDPB)

articles.assessTrigger: Has your organization identified all automated decision-making processes that produce legal or similarly significant effects, and for those that rely on an exception, is meaningful human review genuinely built into the process rather than notional?

gapRemediation.smb: If you use any automated scoring, screening, or decisioning tool, even a third-party SaaS product, assess whether it produces decisions with significant effects on individuals and document that assessment.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Map all automated decision-making processes, assess each for Article 22 applicability, document the applicable exception and safeguards, and build a genuine human review step where required.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise Article 22 programs require a formal inventory of automated decision-making systems, documented exception grounds for each, defined human review processes with evidence of genuine engagement, and a mechanism for data subjects to contest decisions. AI governance frameworks should be integrated with your Article 22 compliance program.

articles.surfaceLabel: Keeping Track of Everything You Do With Personal Data
articles.plainSummary: Most organizations are required to maintain a detailed internal record of every way they use personal data, who they share it with, why they have it, and how long they keep it. This record must be available to regulators on request.
articles.personalImpact: You cannot protect what no one is tracking. Article 30 requires companies to keep a written record of how they use your data. When a regulator asks, the company cannot claim it lost track. That record is what makes real accountability possible.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 30 requires controllers and processors to maintain records of processing activities. Controller records must include the name and contact details of the controller and DPO, purposes of processing, data subject categories and personal data categories, recipients or categories of recipients, international transfer details, and, where possible, retention periods and security measures. Records must be provided to the supervisory authority on request. Organizations with fewer than 250 employees are exempt unless the processing is likely to pose a risk, is not occasional, or includes special category data or criminal conviction data. The RoPA is the operational backbone of GDPR compliance. Virtually every other obligation depends on its accuracy.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization maintain a current, accurate RoPA that maps every processing activity to its legal basis, retention period, and recipient categories, and is it reviewed when processing changes?

gapRemediation.smb: Even organizations below the 250-employee threshold likely need a RoPA in practice. A simple spreadsheet covering your main processing activities is a defensible starting point. Semi-annual review as your processing evolves is recommended.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your RoPA should be a living document integrated with your privacy program. It drives your breach response, your DSR fulfillment, and your legal basis documentation. Ownership should be assigned and review cycles defined.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise RoPA programs require dedicated tooling, privacy management software or a structured database, that integrates with your business systems. The RoPA should update automatically when new processing is approved. DPO oversight of RoPA accuracy is standard.

articles.surfaceLabel: Does Your Company Need a Privacy Officer?
articles.plainSummary: Some organizations are required by law to appoint a dedicated privacy officer called a Data Protection Officer. Even when not legally required, many organizations appoint one voluntarily as a sign of commitment to privacy.
articles.personalImpact: Inside an organization, someone should ask whether a new data practice is even lawful. Articles 37 to 39 require a data protection officer to do exactly that. They handle your concerns and challenge risky uses from within. You gain a dedicated contact responsible for protecting your rights.
articles.professionalLayer: Articles 37 through 39 establish the mandatory DPO requirement. DPO appointment is mandatory for public authorities, except courts acting in their judicial capacity. It is also mandatory where core activities involve regular and systematic monitoring of individuals on a large scale. The same applies where core activities involve large-scale processing of special category data or criminal conviction data. EU or national law can require more. Germany, for example, requires a DPO where at least 20 people constantly handle automated processing of personal data. The DPO must have expert knowledge of data protection law, must be provided with resources, must report to the highest management level, must not receive instructions on how to exercise their tasks, and must not be dismissed or penalized for performing their role. Controllers and processors must publish DPO contact details and communicate them to their supervisory authority.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization meet the mandatory DPO threshold, and if not, have you documented the assessment confirming the threshold does not apply?

gapRemediation.smb: Assess the threshold criteria carefully, including national rules that can lower the bar, as in Germany. If you do not meet them, document that assessment. If you do, appointment is mandatory regardless of cost.
gapRemediation.midMarket: At this scale the threshold question is often borderline. A formal threshold assessment reviewed by legal counsel is recommended. Whether mandatory or voluntary, a privacy lead with defined responsibilities is good practice.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise organizations subject to the mandatory threshold must appoint a qualified DPO with genuine independence. The DPO function should have dedicated resources, executive access, and a defined escalation path to the board.

articles.surfaceLabel: Checking the Privacy Risks Before You Start
articles.plainSummary: Before starting any new activity that could create significant privacy risks, organizations must conduct a formal privacy risk assessment. This process helps identify and reduce risks before they cause harm.
articles.personalImpact: A company wants to scan every face at the door or log your every click. Article 35 requires it to weigh the risk to you before turning that on. Dangerous ideas get caught on paper, not on your data. Risks are assessed and reduced before they can affect you.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment, referred to throughout this site as a PIA, before processing that is likely to result in high risk to individuals, particularly where new technologies are used. A PIA is always required for systematic and extensive profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. It is also required for large-scale special category or criminal data, and for large-scale monitoring of public areas. Each supervisory authority also publishes its own list of operations that need one. The assessment must include a systematic description of the processing, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, an assessment of risks to data subjects, and measures to address those risks. Where a PIA indicates high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, the controller must consult the supervisory authority before proceeding. A PIA is also considered best practice for any significant change to existing processing.

sourceLinks.label: Article 29 Working Party guidelines on DPIAs (endorsed by the EDPB)

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization have a defined trigger list for when a PIA is required, and a process to complete one before high-risk processing begins rather than after?

gapRemediation.smb: Identify your highest-risk processing activities and document a basic PIA for each. Your supervisory authority's published PIA list is a good starting point. A PIA does not need to be complex to be defensible at this scale.
gapRemediation.midMarket: A PIA template and a defined trigger list should be part of your privacy program. PIAs should be required before any new product, system, or significant change to existing processing. Privacy review should be embedded in your project intake process.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise PIA programs require integration with your project management and product development processes. PIAs should be tracked, versioned, and reviewed by the DPO. Residual risk decisions should be documented and escalated appropriately.

articles.surfaceLabel: What Happens When Your Data Is Compromised
articles.plainSummary: If a breach exposes your personal information, the company must report it to the regulator within 72 hours. It can skip this only if the breach is unlikely to put people at risk. If the breach is likely to cause you serious harm, it must also tell you directly.
articles.personalImpact: A breach spills your passwords and ID onto the open web. The worst response a company can give is silence. Articles 33 and 34 require it to alert the regulator within 72 hours when people could be at risk. It must also warn you when the risk is high. You are notified in time to secure your accounts.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 33 requires notice to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach. No notice is needed if the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals. A late notice must give reasons for the delay. Processors must tell their controllers without undue delay. The notice must describe the breach, the people and records affected, the DPO or other contact point, likely consequences, and measures taken or proposed. Controllers must document every breach, notified or not. Article 34 requires telling affected data subjects without undue delay where the risk is likely to be high. That notice is not needed if the data was unintelligible, for example encrypted, or if later measures removed the high risk. Where individual notice would take disproportionate effort, a public notice can replace it. The 72-hour clock starts from awareness, so detection capability is the main operational challenge.
articles.responseTimeline: Supervisory authority: without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness, unless the breach is unlikely to cause a risk. Data subjects: without undue delay where the risk is high.

sourceLinks.label: EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification

articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization have a documented breach response plan that defines awareness, includes a 72-hour notification workflow, and assigns clear ownership for supervisory authority and data subject notification decisions?

gapRemediation.smb: A documented breach response checklist covering detection, containment, assessment, and notification is a reasonable starting point. The 72-hour clock waits for no one. Knowing who to call and what to do before a breach happens is critical.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your breach response plan should be tested annually. A defined severity matrix helps teams quickly assess whether supervisory authority and data subject notification are required. Legal counsel should be identified in advance.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise breach response requires a cross-functional incident response team, integrated detection and logging systems, pre-drafted notification templates, and regular tabletop exercises. Regulatory relationships with lead supervisory authorities should be established before a breach occurs.

comparisonFlags.note: PIPL requires immediate notification with no fixed hour threshold.
LGPD requires notification within 3 business days, a different timeline from GDPR's 72 hours.

articles.plainSummary: Moving personal information out of the European Economic Area is only allowed under specific conditions. The receiving country must provide an adequate level of protection, or the organization must put specific legal safeguards in place.
articles.personalImpact: Your data rarely stays where you live. It flows to servers abroad under different rules. Articles 44 to 49 require your protection to travel with it, which is why EU-to-US transfers have faced years of court challenges. Your safeguards continue to apply wherever the data goes.
articles.professionalLayer: Chapter V restricts transfers of personal data to third countries or international organizations unless an adequate level of protection is ensured. The primary transfer mechanisms are adequacy decisions (Article 45), Standard Contractual Clauses (Article 46), Binding Corporate Rules (Article 47), and derogations for specific situations (Article 49). Transfers within the European Economic Area are not restricted. The GDPR has applied in Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein since July 2018. The Schrems II decision in July 2020 invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield. It required exporters using SCCs to check, case by case, whether the destination country undermines that protection. That check is now known as a Transfer Impact Assessment. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework, adopted in July 2023, is an adequacy decision for certified US recipients. The General Court upheld it in September 2025, and an appeal is pending at the Court of Justice. In June 2026 the US Supreme Court ended for-cause protection for FTC commissioners in Trump v. Slaughter. In July 2026 the EDPB asked the Commission to assess the effect on the framework, which remains in force. International transfers represent one of the highest-risk areas of GDPR compliance for multinational organizations.
articles.assessTrigger: Has your organization mapped every international data transfer and confirmed that each relies on a valid transfer mechanism, including completing a Transfer Impact Assessment where SCCs are used?

gapRemediation.smb: Identify every country your data flows to, including cloud services, SaaS platforms, and third-party processors. Confirm each transfer relies on a valid mechanism. SCCs with a completed TIA are the most common approach for small organizations.
gapRemediation.midMarket: A transfer mapping exercise integrated with your RoPA is the foundation. Each transfer should be documented with its mechanism and a completed TIA where required. Vendor contracts should be reviewed for SCC inclusion.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise international transfer programs require systematic mapping across all business units, automated TIA workflows, centralized SCC management, and active monitoring of adequacy decisions and legal challenges. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework status requires ongoing monitoring.

comparisonFlags.note: PIPL requires a CAC security assessment for high-volume handlers, a government-administered process with no GDPR equivalent.
